 Los Angeles On-Location Production Declines Again Even As California’s Tax Incentive Heavily Backs Remaining Projects
 By Katie Campione 
 Katie Campione 
 Senior TV & Labor Reporter

 On-location production is still declining in the Los Angeles area, even if California’s Film & Television Tax Credit Program is propping up much of what’s left.
 Per the latest report from FilmLA , on-location filming accounted for 4,171 shoot days from July through September 2026, which is a 4.8% decrease from the same period last year. However, the organization also finds that the state’s tax incentive is accounting for about 40.3% of scripted, on-location production during that time — nearly doubling the share from a year ago.

 Television is benefitting the most from incentivized productions. Projects that were accepted into the program made up 62% of all TV comedy shoot days and 49.4% of TV drama shoot days (up from 19% and 20.6%, respectively) during the same time last year. 
 This doesn’t quite tell the full story, since television production, particularly on comedies, often largely takes place on soundstages, which are not captured in this data. Soundstage occupancy also remains far below the levels it once maintained a decade ago.
 Watch on Deadline 
 Incentivized TV series that shot in L.A. last quarter included A Hundred Percent (Netflix), Baywatch (Fox), Mr & Mrs. Smith (Amazon), Shrinking (Warner Bros. TV/Apple TV+), High Potential (ABC), The Night Agent (Sony Pictures Television/Netflix), Tracker (CBS), I Love LA (HBO), and Rooster (HBO).
 Feature films finished the third quarter with 533 shoot days, a marginal 2.1% increase from the same period last year. Incentivized projects account for 24.4% of that total, the majority of which are independent. However, there are a few studio films in the mix including 13 Going on 30 (Netflix), Cut Off (Warner Bros.) and They Follow (Neon).
 Commercials marked the largest decline, down 15.9% to on-location 562 shoot days during the third quarter, although those are not covered by California’s tax credit program.
 On-location production in Los Angeles has been on a decline for years , and the trend has continued despite California’s massive efforts to expand the state’s tax incentive program last year. Not only did lawmakers raise the cap to $750 million annually, the revamped bill also significantly expanded program eligibility. Granted, this quarter’s decline is smaller than Q2’s 13% slip .

 Getting a grip 
 on October 22, 2026 3:43 am 
 Many of the commenters here are living in a bubble. Production is down EVERYWHERE. And if you live in a small city, and a rando film or series project rolls in, it’s easy to think, “Sorry, LA! We’re popping!” 
 Talk to anyone from California to Oregon to Albuquerque to NY to Atlanta, and there’s just less work, period. And yes, even in the UK where much of the boom has been (since the strikes, thank you), it’s down. What’s up are verticals which pay next to nothing and – good lord, have you watched any of these things? Ack. Best advice for newbies is to get in with anyone making Tik-Tok or YouTube projects and live frugally. Oh, and be willing to relocate on a dime (abroad as well).
